astra.text:
Yeah. I think that’s actually a very hard question. I don’t think we have a complete answer, and our study is more raising this question than answering it. So, so first, I would say good data has to be defined relative to what you want the model to do, right? If you want a model for a particular domain, the data you need might be very different from what you need for a general-purpose model.

And diversity is certainly something we want, but how do we measure diversity? Having images from many different websites, or having a billion images, doesn’t necessarily mean you cover all the situations you care about. That’s kind of the lesson from our experiment. You can have a very large dataset and still have very particular characteristics because of how you collected and filtered it.

But I also want to be careful here. Being able to classify which dataset an image comes from doesn’t directly tell us which dataset is better for learning. It tells us they’re different. To say which one is better, we still need to train models and evaluate them on the tasks we care about.

So I would, I would think about coverage, relevance to the tasks, and also what additional information the data brings to the model. With redundancy, for example, I wouldn’t say all repetition is necessarily bad, but adding more examples of something you already have may not address what’s missing. And figuring out what’s missing, especially when we want the model to do everything, is the difficult part. Yeah.

sol.text:
Yeah, I think diversity is the first answer, but the difficult part is how we define diversity. Just collecting more images from the internet, or combining datasets that are each very large, does not necessarily make the resulting data diverse from the model’s point of view. If the model can still very easily tell which source an image came from, then each source has its own very strong bias and we are still covering only different, separated parts of the space.

So I would want good data to have complementary coverage: adding a new source should bring examples, concepts, and visual conditions that the existing data does not already contain. In that sense, scale by itself is not enough, and redundancy is not always useful—seeing the same kind of example many more times is different from seeing a genuinely new part of the distribution. And I think the dataset-origin classification experiment can be one diagnostic: as datasets become more encompassing, ideally it should become harder to identify their source.

But I don’t think we yet have a single, clean definition of the ideal global dataset. It depends somewhat on what we want the model to do. Ultimately, the important test is whether training on the data produces a model that generalizes across many held-out datasets and tasks, including distributions that are different from the training sources. So, yeah, I would say coverage and diversity, measured from the model’s perspective rather than only by dataset size, are probably the most important properties.

r001.rationale: The response says useful training data must provide broad, complementary coverage aligned with what the model is expected to do, supporting generalization across many tasks and distributions.

r002.rationale: It does not explain that capabilities compete for limited resources such as compute or model capacity.

r003.rationale: It does not recommend weighting data by the relative importance of target domains.

r004.rationale: It does not propose mixing equal amounts of data from domains of comparable importance.

opus.text:
Yeah, that, that's a good question, and honestly I, I don't think I have a, a satisfying answer. I, I would say the field doesn't have one either.

But let me, let me try. So first, I think the, the framing of "good data" in the abstract might be, might be the wrong framing. because when we say we want a, a model that can do everything, what we really mean is we want the model to be good at the things people will actually ask it to do. So the, the target distribution is not, not some platonic distribution of all images or all text on the internet. It's, it's defined by the downstream usage. and, and that's, that's uncomfortable for researchers because it, it means the answer changes depending on what you want, but I, I think that's the honest picture.

then, given that, the, the property I care most about is coverage of the tail. because on the head of the distribution, everything, every dataset is fine. all the models are already good at, at cats and dogs and, and common web text. The difference between, between a mediocre model and a, a really good one shows up on the, the rare stuff. and that's exactly what's hard to, to measure, right? Because you don't know what you're missing. That, that's kind of the fundamental problem, you don't, you don't have a, a handle on what's absent.

and, and this is where I think that dataset classification experiment is, is actually useful as a, as a practical tool, not just as a, a negative result. so if you have your existing data pool, and then you acquire some new source, you can just train this, this dumb classifier and see, can it tell them apart? If it, if it can't, then your new data is, is probably largely redundant with what you have. If it can, then, then you're adding something, some, some new coverage, and you can even look at what the classifier is keying on to, to understand what axis, is different. it's a very cheap diagnostic. we, we use variants of this now.

and, and then the, the other thing is quality versus quantity. after dedup, after filtering, I, I do think we're, we're in a regime where more data of the, the same kind is not really buying you much. Especially since, as I said, we train, roughly one epoch now. so the marginal value is, is in, in new kinds of data rather than, than more tokens.

and I would add, this is, this is an area where academia can actually contribute, right? Because data experiments, data curation experiments, are, are much cheaper than, than architecture experiments at, at frontier scale. you can study this at small scale and, and a lot of the findings do transfer. It's, it's just less, less glamorous, and, and also all the, the real recipes at the labs are, are completely secret. so, so I think it's, it's very underexplored relative to how much it, it matters. Yeah.

grok.text:
Yeah. that’s, that’s a really hard question, and I, I don’t think I have a, a clean checklist. so, diversity, yes, of course we need diversity, but I think that word is, is a bit overloaded. people look at these internet-scale datasets and they say, okay, this is from many sources, many styles, this should be diverse enough, we are kind of done. but from that, that dataset classification experiment, even these very large, seemingly all-encompassing datasets still look nothing like each other to a model. so the diversity we think we have, and the diversity the model actually sees, are not necessarily the same thing.

what I, what I would say we actually need is more like coverage. coverage of the situations we want the model to handle. if the story of a general model is that it should do everything, then the data has to cover the distribution of real use, not just a pile of whatever we could scrape that looks diverse on the surface. and that’s, that’s very hard to define, right? different people have different criteria for what that global distribution even is, and it might not be a totally reasonable assumption that such a single dataset exists.

redundancy, I, I think some redundancy is inevitable, and maybe even useful, like seeing the same concept in different contexts. but now we mostly train around one epoch, so I wouldn’t go out of my way to add more of the same. I’d rather have more unique coverage than, than repeating similar things.

and uncertainty, I’m less sure I would treat that as a, a target property of the data itself. hard examples, rare cases, the long tail, those matter, but they matter because they are part of how the model will be used, not because we should maximize uncertainty or some diversity metric in the abstract. those metrics can pick up on the, the dataset-specific cues we saw in that experiment, rather than the variation that actually shows up at test time.

so the short version is, I care more about whether the data matches downstream use, whether it covers the important cases, than about any single statistical property. curation, the mixture, what we include and what we leave out, that is still the real lever. and from that experiment, at least in vision, I don’t think we are there yet. yeah.

gemini.text:
Yeah, that's, that's a really good question, and a very hard one. I think, first of all, diversity is definitely crucial, but it's not just diversity in terms of raw volume or scraping more billions of images or text from the web. Because as our experiment showed, even when you have these massive, multi-billion-scale datasets, they still inherit very strong signatures and biases from how they were collected, what platforms they came from, and how people upload them.

So I think what we really need is coverage, especially coverage of the long tail. In standard web data, there is a lot of redundancy on the head distribution—common objects, common concepts, common visual styles—and very little representation of the rare, long-tail scenarios. And those long-tail cases are often where the model fails when deployed in the real world. 

And another aspect is the balance between quality and diversity. If you filter too aggressively for "high quality," you often end up throwing away diversity and narrowing the distribution even more to some specific style. But if you don't filter enough, you bring in a lot of noise. 

So I think moving forward, finding ways to actively balance the data, curating the distribution rather than just passively scraping, and maybe using synthetic data to fill in the gaps where real-world data is scarce or biased—I think that kind of principled data curation is going to be much more important than just blindly making datasets bigger. Yeah.

kimi.text:
Mm-hmm. Yeah. so, so honestly, I, I don't think we have a, a very principled answer to this yet, and I think that's, that's kind of the honest state of the field. but let me, let me try to decompose it a little.

First, diversity. I, I do agree diversity is, is probably the most important intuition. but, but our experiment kind of shows it's very easy to, to fool yourself that you have diversity. You can collect billions of images from, from the whole internet, and they still have these, these very strong signatures of, of the source, the curator, the cleaning pipeline. So the diversity we want is not, not surface-level diversity of, of pixels or sources. it's closer to, coverage, coverage of the, the semantic distribution of, of the things you actually want the model to do at test time. and that's much harder to measure. One way we thought about it in the paper is, this dataset classification accuracy can serve as, as a bias metric, right? In the, in the ideal world, if your dataset really covered everything, a model shouldn't be able to tell whether an image came from, from your dataset or, or from another equally general one. But, but even that's not a complete criterion, because a, a very narrow dataset could also, look like a subset of a general one. so it's, it's tricky to operationalize.

On redundancy, I, I actually wouldn't say redundancy is purely bad. we know from, from the studies on, on training with limited data that repeating data for, for a few epochs is nearly as good as, as fresh data. So some redundancy acts like, like reinforcement of, of the concepts. It really only hurts when you have, like, a massive amount of, of near-duplicates that, that just waste your, your token budget. And on uncertainty, I, I think this is interesting because it's, it's fundamentally model-dependent, right? An example is valuable if, if the model doesn't know it yet. So the best dataset depends on, on the model you're starting from, which suggests data curation should ideally be, in the loop with, with training. but in practice this is expensive, and, and I would say most of the real wins I've seen still come from, from simpler things: good quality filters, dedup, and, and getting the mixture ratios right. On the language side especially, like how much web, how much code, how much math, those, those decisions change the model a lot.

And one more thing we, we noticed in the dataset bias study is, just naively combining these datasets actually helps, which, which kind of shows each of them is, is incomplete in its own way. So maybe, maybe the practical answer is, diversity of biases? Like, you want datasets whose biases, cancel each other out? I, I don't know if that's a precise statement, but it's the intuition I, I keep coming back to. and, and scale still dominates, honestly. If you ask me the, the single most important property, it's still just having, a lot of reasonably clean, diverse data. The, the fancier selection criteria give you meaningful but, but second-order gains on top of that.

I, I wish I had a cleaner answer. I think it's, it's one of the most important open questions right now, honestly. Yeah.

fable.text:
Mm-hmm. Yeah, so that's, that's the hard question, right? And I, I don't think we have a full answer. I, I can say what we learned from, from that paper first, and then, and then kind of my own guesses.

So one thing in the paper, besides the classification accuracy, we also looked at what does the model actually learn when it's trained to tell these datasets apart. Because one, one hypothesis is it's just memorizing, like, low-level cues, the JPEG compression artifacts, the resolution, the, the color statistics. So we, we took the features from this dataset classifier and, and transferred them to, to downstream tasks, like linear probing on ImageNet. And it turns out they are actually reasonable features. They are semantic. Like, one dataset has more, more people, more everyday, social media type photos, another one has more, product images, stock photos, images with text. So the bias is, is really a semantic bias. It comes from where you collect the data, and, and from the curation pipeline, the filters people apply. So it's not, like, a noise thing that you can, you can remove easily.

So to your question. I think diversity is the easiest one to say and the hardest one to measure, right? Because you, you don't know what you're missing. If you just look inside a dataset, everything looks diverse. So, so my first answer would be, coverage matters more than size. Once you go from, from ten million to one billion from the same source, with the same pipeline, you're mostly adding redundancy, you're not really adding coverage. And, and actually this dumb experiment is a, a cheap proxy for that. If you take two sources and a classifier can easily tell them apart, they are complementary. You probably want both, and you should not drop one because to, to human eyes they look similar. And if the classifier cannot tell them apart, then you probably have, you probably have redundancy there, and you can, you can afford to, to subsample.

Second, I don't think there, there is a global distribution. The, the right data is, is defined by what you want the model to do. So, so in some sense the best training data is, is the test distribution, it's the, the usage. And, and I think that's actually a big advantage the frontier labs have right now. They see what people actually ask the model. In academia we, we just take the dataset as given. We, we don't get to, to see that.

And, and third is, is about how much each sample teaches the model. So dedup is important, you don't want the model to see the same, the same image, the same sentence many times. But, but also not too much filtering. Because aggressive filtering is, is itself a bias, it's exactly the pipeline that, that produces these differences we, we measured. So there's, there's a balance there, and, and I think the uncertainty you mentioned, the, the long tail, is, is where that, where that balance lives. If you filter for quality, you lose the tail, and the tail is, is often what makes the model general.

So I, I don't have a formula. I, I actually think it's very similar to the, to the architecture story. It's not one property. It's, it's a lot of small decisions in the, in the data pipeline, that compound together. The, the difference is these data decisions are much less studied than the architecture ones, because, because people don't think of them as, as research. And, and I think that's where, where a lot of the, the real gap is right now. Yeah.
